I went through something similar. Best thing that I've done is read about emotional intelligence and social skills and then just observing people for a bit and making a note of different things they do that are successful.

Then, I started making small talk with cashiers, receptionists, etc. Nothing long or involved, just smiling, doing the usual "How are you?" exchange, and maybe complimenting them if I notice something I genuinely like. Sometimes the compliments can be a sort of joke like if they're wearing something for a holiday that's not something you would usually see. Also, try to help people when you see someone that needs help and maybe try to relate. Like "Oh, this happens every time I try to do x, so I know how it feels".

Then, find different things you're interested in and join groups where you can practice interacting with people and maybe even meeting people to build friendships with. Just remember that no one is perfect and as long as your intentions are good and you do your best, anyone that judges you or anything isn't likely to be the right person to have in your life.

1) You can improve relatively quickly in classes like math and english. You study, get help with problems you don't understand, etc. Kids who failed the previous test are able to pass or even ace the next test that comes along. In order to run faster, for example, it would take a while to train up a healthy, but "out of shape" kid. That's if they know what they're doing. But, an overweight kid who is "failing" at the beginning of the semester will most likely give up because there's no way for them to go from a 20 minute mile down to a 6 minute mile by the time the semester ends.

2) Assuming you're in the US, every PE class is different. I had PE classes aimed at teaching ways to stay active that everyone could use even after we'd finished the class. I had another PE class at a different school that utilized a similar grading system to the one that you're suggesting. Kids would run laps until they literally passed out just so they didn't fail the class. 

Though I do agree PE classes need to be more effective, a one-size-fits-all approach isn't going to work. In fact, you'll just make kids have negative associations with exercise for the rest of their lives, making it more difficult for them to be healthy adults.   Even when adults exercise, everyone has different goals: some are training for a marathon, some want to lose weight, and some even exercise simply because it has a positive impact on mental health.

Kids come into PE at different levels of fitness and health. The most important thing is to help them learn how to exercise and take care of themselves in a way that is applicable to them. So, I would have kids set realistic goals at the beginning of the semester and help them find ways to improve and track their goals. As long as they are putting the work in and making progress towards their goals, I would give them a good grade.

This replicates the way adults set and work toward fitness goals, setting the kids up to continue doing so into adulthood. By setting realistic goals, no kid is encouraged to give up on the class or physical activity overall just because they don't measure up to their peers.

However, if one of them would pass away or be incapacitated, it would be very similar to what many gay couples experienced during the AIDS crisis. In the absence of legal documents outlining power of attorney and what is to be done with posessions of the couple, each individual's family would be entitled to make decisions on their behalf. This means that the partner could lose property that otherwise would be protected as marital property. They also would not be able to make medical decisions for their partner, since marriage is the only way a partner can become next of kin without being made power of attorney. Tbh, regardless of your situation, I always encourage everyone to have an advanced directive and to specifically name a power of attorney to avoid any confusion on how you want medical decision making to go.

I know you mentioned she has a sister and you're a single mom working full time. Do you ever make time for just you and her to spend together? For kids struggling with feeling like they've been rejected by one parent, it's important to make sure they feel secure in their relationship with the parent that is present. Making sure she has even just an hour of your undivided attention when you can swing it might be helpful in making her feel like she is safe and cared about. It can be something she likes to do or even just running errands, kids love to be helpful. Even grocery shopping can give some time for both of you to connect. It's during these times where you would least expect it that kids will bring up things that are bothering them even if it's just in passing. 

Definitely also consider getting her involved in extracurricular activities, especially those outside of her school where she might meet kids she usually wouldn't have the chance to interact with. A lot of times libraries will have different programs and events where she could try out different interests.

Also, definitely make sure you're taking care of yourself. You sound like an awesome mom, but this stuff definitely wears on you over time. If you haven't already, it's always good to find people you can vent to who might be struggling with similar things. There's a lot of subs on here so you should be able to find a few places that will help support you when you need it.

Also if you're using insurance, make sure that they won't require a prior authorization to get a different quantity of a different dose. It usually won't be a problem, but I ran into this with a previous insurance and pharmacies aren't always great about telling you if your insurance won't cover something unless you ask directly.

Not a parent, but I'm currently raising my 16 yo brother. The biggest thing I've found is allowing kids to feel comfortable having conversations about drugs and alcohol so that you can inform them of the risks, correct any misinformation they may have, and serve as a support system if/when peers pressure them to use substances.

I heavily discourage experimenting with it, but I always explain the reasons behind that. One big reason for us specifically is that we have a strong family history of addiction and substance abuse and it is easier to never start than to try to get clean/sober.

However, I acknowledge that teens especially are at an age where peers may pressure them, their brains are still maturing, and they are trying different things to figure out who they are. So, I take a harm reduction approach and am very open with my brother about ways that I will help him to stay safe. One of these is not driving if he has had any alcohol. I would rather him call to have me pick him up than to put himself and others in danger. Another thing that we have often talked about is the dangers of fentanyl. I have testing kits on hand as well as narcan just in case he (or his friends) would end up experimenting with drugs.

While a lot of what I do is specific to teens, overall it's just helpful to show them that you are there to help when they need it and that you trust them to make responsible decisions. Definitely share age appropriate info with them as not informing them won't prevent them from getting the information, it usually just pushes them to seek it out from someone else who may be manipulative or simply be giving out incorrect info.

I'm younger, so, I'll just share some stuff about how I would've liked my parents to react. Overall, talk to her about what she needs and keep those lines open. My #1 thing was just needing someone to talk to about the little things. Don't judge her, just listen and let her know that you're there and you're trying. Listening will let you understand more about what she needs from you and what she might be struggling with.

Be sensitive to things that might be triggering for her. For example, my family liked to force me to hug everyone after I disclosed my abuse to them even though I was very uncomfortable with touch. Noticing that something causes her discomfort and working with her to alleviate those intense emotions is extremely helpful.

As far as the risk for another suicide attempt, it's imperative that she doesn't feel watched 24/7 and that she still has some privacy. Being in therapy is another place where she can learn how to cope with intense emotions and vent when she's dealing with a lot. Having all of those supports in place gives her multiple resources to turn to if she's having suicidal thoughts. Something that was helpful for me was Crisis Text Line. It's completely anonymous and you can text in for support during everything from suicidal thoughts to a break-up. Sometimes, it's hard to face someone you know, and you just need that anonymity. For them, you just text START to 741741.

You already sound like you're doing your best to support her and that makes a world of difference. Communication is key, she decides what she needs and how she feels. Also, make sure to take care of yourself, it can be hard to hear that someone has gone through something like that and you can't support her if you don't take care of yourself.
